name: Aisha Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at the Kestrel nickel mine, what we call a bogger. It scoops the broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass, back and forth, about eight hundred metres below the surface. I start with the cage ride down at a quarter to seven, and the best part is getting a clean draw point, when the bucket fills in one go. The worst part is the heat down there and the noise in your teeth by the end of the day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, Tomas, in a flat above the bakery on Mill Street in Ashby. He's a care worker at the aged care home, so neither of us is rich. We've got maybe three weeks of money put away, and my sister's wedding next year is already eating into that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be fine by me, honestly. We've been told something big is coming for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing I say about every new gadget the company buys: let's see if it works before we fire anyone. At the union meeting I'd probably make a joke about the expensive chatbot that can't drive a bogger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Underneath, I'd be relieved. My job stays, pay stays low, nothing gets better either. That's the part people forget: no change also means no raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep chipping away at savings, maybe a hundred a month after the wedding. I'd probably use the AI thing on my phone now and then for the boring paperwork, like the pre-start forms. And I'd keep going to the union to push for the heat allowance we've been asking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe. It's not a dream, but it's not a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no change means no raise. What would a raise actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean we could move out of the flat above the bakery, which smells amazing at four in the morning until you've smelled it for two years. And it'd mean I could say yes to Tomas about a holiday without doing sums in my head first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use the AI tools much now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I asked one to help me write a complaint about the ventilation on level twelve, and it was better than what I'd have written. I don't trust it with anything that could hurt someone, though.

S0.say: She'd say let's see if the new tools work before anyone gets fired, and would joke at the union meeting about the expensive chatbot that can't drive a loader.
S0.think: She'd be relieved her job stays, but points out that no change also means pay stays low and nothing gets better. A raise would mean a better flat and less money stress.
S0.do: Keeps working and saves about a hundred a month after her sister's wedding. Uses AI now and then for paperwork and keeps pushing through the union for a heat allowance.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, neither a dream nor a nightmare.
S0.quote: That's the part people forget: no change also means no raise.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha sees the calm scenario through the lens of low pay rather than job safety: stability isn't progress for her. She already uses AI for small paperwork tasks, but draws a firm line at anything safety-related. Her union involvement is about everyday conditions like heat and ventilation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one feels real. They already have tele-remote boggers at a couple of the other mines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say it can be good if it's done fairly, because nobody actually loves breathing diesel at eight hundred metres. But I'd say it loudly that the people underground now should get first go at the surface jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is that one person in a control room can run three loaders, so two of us lose out. Where I sit depends on whether the company trains us or just hires younger people who grew up on video games.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the tele-remote training the first time it's offered, once a few people have done it and it's not a mess. I'd ask the union to get a promise in writing that current operators get first pick. And I'd cut the takeaway nights and stop paying for the second phone plan, so we have a bit more of a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Part of me likes the idea of a job with air conditioning. Part of me is counting the chairs in that control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others to do the training first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the company roll things out half-baked. The new fleet-tracking tablets froze for three months and people got written up for it. I'd let someone else find the bugs, then jump in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who's been on the boggers for twenty years and can't stand screens. He's the best operator I know by feel, and none of that counts in a control room. I'd probably end up helping him with the tablet and feeling guilty about it.

S1.say: She'd say automation can be good if it's fair, since nobody loves breathing diesel underground, but would loudly insist current workers get first go at the new surface jobs.
S1.think: She believes one control-room operator can run three loaders, so two people lose out. Whether she survives depends on the company training current staff rather than hiring young gamers.
S1.do: Signs up for tele-remote training once a few others have tested it, and asks the union for a written promise that current operators get first pick. Cuts takeaway nights and a second phone plan to build a small buffer.
S1.feel: Uneasy, drawn to an air-conditioned job but counting the chairs in the control room.
S1.quote: Part of me likes the idea of a job with air conditioning. Part of me is counting the chairs in that control room.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha is a careful adopter: she wants the new job but lets others find the bugs first, based on a real bad rollout. Her progressive view shows in insisting that current workers get first claim. She worries about an older colleague more than she lets on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then it's not three loaders per person in a control room, is it. It's no person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in now, not after. Pay people while they find their feet, and make the companies that profit pay for it. I'd be sharing union posts, and I'd probably be at a rally in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. We've got three weeks of money and Tomas's job doesn't cover the rent on its own. If robots reach hands-on work too, then even his job at the care home isn't safe forever, so it's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister we're scaling back the wedding gift and we'd stop all the extras the same week. I'd still try for any control-room job going, because even a year of that pay helps. And I'd apply for every bit of government support and lean on the union to bargain for a payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the cage dropping too fast. My stomach goes. I don't sleep well thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years let you do that one year wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost nothing, that's the honest answer. Maybe finish a short course, but in what? I'd spend most of the two years just trying to hold on to the paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Tomas stay in Ashby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, his mum is here and she's not well. But if the mine shuts or goes robot, Ashby is just the bakery and the pub. We'd probably end up back with my parents in the city, which neither of us wants.

S2.say: She'd say the government must act now, paying people while they adjust and making profiting companies fund it. She'd share union posts and likely go to a rally in the city.
S2.think: She's scared because she and her partner have three weeks of savings and his care work could be at risk too once robots reach hands-on jobs. Two years leaves almost no time to do anything but hold on.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding gift and all extras straight away, still goes for any control-room job for the pay, and applies for every government support available. Pushes the union to bargain for a payout.
S2.feel: Like the cage dropping too fast; her stomach goes and she doesn't sleep well.
S2.quote: Two years? Then it's not three loaders per person in a control room, is it. It's no person.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline breaks Aisha's usual 'wait until it's proven' strategy, because there's no time to wait. She worries about her partner's job as well as her own, which doubles the household risk. Moving back to her parents' place in the city is the outcome she most wants to avoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still quick, but you'd at least get to watch it happen to other mines first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when we organise, while there's time. I'd want a deal across the whole region, not just Kestrel, about retraining and who keeps jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is that five years is enough to get one new skill, if I start early. Not enough for a whole new life. I'd have to pick right the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the tele-remote course and also start an electrical apprenticeship pathway the union's been talking about, part-time. I'd set up an automatic transfer of fifty a week into savings, even if it hurts. By year three I'd be watching what the robot maintenance crews actually need and aim for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. It's like knowing the blast is at two o'clock instead of not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch other mines first. What would you be looking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the people who went to the control room kept their jobs a year later. If they did, I'd go hard at it. If they got cut again, I'd put everything into the electrical side instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister about her wedding, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll still be there and still dance badly. But the gift might be a framed photo instead of the kitchen mixer she wants. She'd laugh, she knows.

S3.say: She'd say it's time to organise while there's time, pushing for a region-wide deal on retraining and who keeps jobs, not just at her own mine.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to gain one new skill if she starts early, but not a whole new life, so she has to choose right the first time.
S3.do: Takes the tele-remote course and starts a part-time electrical pathway through the union in year one. Sets up an automatic transfer of fifty a week and by year three targets the skills robot maintenance crews need.
S3.feel: Anxious but more in control, like knowing when the blast is scheduled.
S3.quote: It's like knowing the blast is at two o'clock instead of not knowing.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Aisha use her natural approach: watch others, then commit. She hedges between two paths and will choose based on evidence from other mines. Her humour about the wedding gift shows how money shapes even small family moments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's enough time to actually plan something, which I've never really been able to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse for anyone ending up on the street. I'd push the union and the council to start a plan for Ashby now, while the mine is still paying taxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more hopeful about this one than I should be. Ten years is long enough to finish an apprenticeship and work a few years as an electrician. I don't know if there are still electricians in 2036, but at least I'd have tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical apprenticeship within a year, part-time while I'm still on the bogger. Tomas and I would put off moving out of the flat and save the difference, maybe a hundred a fortnight. I'd also use AI to help with the study, because I've seen it explain things better than my old teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's hope in it. It's like a long tunnel where you can see a bit of light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you don't trust AI with anything that could hurt someone. Would you trust it with your study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For study, yes, as long as someone checks my work. Explaining Ohm's law to me ten times without getting bored, it's perfect for that. Wiring a live panel, no, that's still on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm choosing instead of getting pushed. With two years I'd grab whatever's left. With ten I could pick something I might actually like.

S4.say: She'd say there's no excuse for anyone ending up on the street after ten years' warning, and would push the union and council to plan for the town while the mine still pays taxes.
S4.think: She's quietly hopeful that ten years is enough to finish an apprenticeship and work as an electrician for a while, though she doesn't know if that job will survive to 2036.
S4.do: Starts a part-time electrical apprenticeship within a year while staying on the loader. Delays moving out of the flat to save about a hundred a fortnight and uses AI to help with study.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, like seeing light at the end of a long tunnel.
S4.quote: It means I'm choosing instead of getting pushed. With two years I'd grab whatever's left.
S4.fieldNote: The extra time turns Aisha from defending her place to planning a career. She's comfortable using AI as a patient tutor while keeping safety work in human hands. She keeps thinking about the town as well as herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years with three weeks of savings and two jobs at risk in one house. What would help is pay while we retrain, and a real plan for towns like Ashby made before the mine changes, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but robots underground could mean fewer people get hurt. I want that too. I just don't want it to cost me my rent.

headlineQuote: I just don't want it to cost me my rent.
portrait: Aisha Yilmaz is a 27-year-old underground loader operator at the Kestrel nickel mine, living above a bakery in Ashby with her partner Tomas, a care worker, on about three weeks of savings. She backs the union, uses AI now and then for paperwork and waits for new things to be proven before jumping in. She's calm about a plateau but annoyed it would mean no raise, and uneasy but interested in tele-remote jobs under steady change. AGI in two years alarms her because both their jobs could go at once, while five and ten years let her plan a move into electrical work. She wants safer mines too, as long as the cost doesn't land on workers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years with three weeks of savings would put both her and her partner's jobs at risk at once.
whatWouldHelp: Pay while people retrain and a real plan for towns like Ashby, made before the mine changes rather than after.
